security_spec.violation_condition: QEMU TCG implements implicit interrupt-entry context save (x10-x15 to stack) in riscv_cpu_do_interrupt() as a non-atomic sequence of guest memory stores, and a higher-priority interrupt arrives mid-save (late preemption), leaving partially-saved or clobbered x10-x15 values on stack that the preempting handler may overwrite before the original save completes. Additionally, if the TCG-generated ipopxret restore uses stack offsets or access sizes that differ from those used during the implicit trap-entry save (both 'implementation defined' per spec), restored x10-x15 values are corrupt.
security_spec.vulnerability_pattern: riscv_cpu_do_interrupt implicit stack write x10-x15 non-atomic + ipopxret stack offset mismatch + late preemption during trap-entry save
security_spec.summary: Smip moves interrupt context save from explicit tpush instruction into implicit trap-entry behavior; QEMU must ensure the implicit stack writes (x10-x15) are consistent with ipopxret restore offsets, atomic with respect to late-preemption, and that removal of xepc/xpistatus from the save frame doesn't leak privileged CSR values through stale stack slots

findings.finding: Smip (implicit x10-x15 save/restore to stack) is not implemented in this QEMU version. riscv_do_nmi() saves only CSR state (mnstatus, mncause, mnepc, MNPELP) and switches to M-mode. There is no implicit stack write of x10-x15 at all, so the 'non-atomic save + late preemption clobber' vulnerability from the security spec does not apply. No popxret/ipopxret instruction exists in the decode tables.

NMI dispatch at interrupt entry correctly checks ext_smrnmi && rnmip before calling riscv_do_nmi(). No implicit GPR save to stack occurs here. The early return (line 2245) correctly short-circuits the normal trap path.

RNMI priority and NMIE gating are correctly implemented. When MNSTATUS_NMIE=0, all interrupts return RISCV_EXCP_NONE, preventing interrupt delivery during NMI handler window. rnmip bits are scanned via ctz64 at top priority, correctly handling multi-source RNMI.

NNMI (nested NMI / M-mode exception while NMIE=0) handling is correct. nnmi_excep is detected (lines 2431-2433, re-evaluated 2466-2468 after hypervisor swap), CFI ELP saved to mnstatus.MNPELP (line 2439), pc set to rnmi_excpvec (line 2504). Double-trap with MDT correctly aborts (line 2478) or routes to riscv_do_nmi (line 2480).

mnret correctly restores PC from mnepc and privilege from MNSTATUS_MNPP without any implicit stack-based GPR restore. Privilege checks via check_ret_from_m_mode (line 464) prevent invalid privilege escalation. NMIE is set to 1 by hardware only (line 468), matching spec. MPRV, DBLTRP, hypervisor swap, and CFI ELP restore are all handled.

NMIE bit is correctly write-protected: hardware-clear-only semantics enforced by line 5510 (env->mnstatus = (env->mnstatus & MNSTATUS_NMIE) | (val & mask)), so software cannot clear NMIE. TLB flush on MNPV change is correct. Mask covers only MNSTATUS_NMIE, MNSTATUS_MNPP, and conditionally MNSTATUS_MNPV.
findings.snippet:
/* mnstatus.mnie can only be cleared by hardware. */
env->mnstatus = (env->mnstatus & MNSTATUS_NMIE) | (val & mask);

findings.finding: RNMI state fields (mnscratch, mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, rnmip, rnmi_irqvec, rnmi_excpvec) are completely absent from VMState in machine.c. Live-migration of a guest with Smrnmi enabled would silently drop all NMI state. After migration, NMIE=1 (wrong), rnmip=0 (lost pending NMIs), mnepc/mncause=0 (lost NMI context). This is data corruption, though distinct from the Smip x10-x15 save/restore concern in the security spec.
findings.snippet: (No rnmip, mnscratch, mnepc, mncause, mnstatus, rnmi_irqvec, or rnmi_excpvec entries found in machine.c)

findings.finding: mnscratch is a simple scratch register (WLRL read/write), so full-value read/write without masking is correct. No reserved bits to enforce.

Reset only clears rnmip and NMIE. Remaining RNMI CSRs (mnscratch, mnepc, mncause, mnstatus non-NMIE fields, rnmi_irqvec, rnmi_excpvec) are not explicitly reset. They rely on zero-initialization of the CPU struct. While practically correct due to g_new0, explicit reset of mnepc/mncause would be more robust against future changes.
